one_liner: Zero-copy UTF-16/UTF-8 string views for AssemblyScript with SIMD/SWAR search; beats stdlib String on search and ASCII case folding.
what_it_does: as-str adds `str`, a view type holding a backing `string` (the GC owner) plus `[start, end)` byte pointers, and `str8`, a byte-indexed UTF-8 view over an ArrayBuffer. It mirrors the AssemblyScript `String` surface (slice, trim, split, indexOf, replace, toUpperCase, comparison operators) both as instance methods and as static free functions that accept a native `string` or a view, so `str.indexOf(s, "x")` can be called on an ordinary string without wrapping it. Results are materialized into a real `string` only on `toString()` or in the allocating ops. Optional compiler transforms (`as-str/global`, `as-str/auto`, `as-str/single`) inject imports or rewrite native-string code into views and packed u64 spans automatically.
how_it_is_fast: Search uses a memchr-style first-code-unit filter (`findUnit`) that tests 8 UTF-16 units per step with `i16x8.eq` + bitmask under `--enable simd`, or 4 units per step with Mycroft's SWAR zero-lane trick on u64 words otherwise, then confirms the tail with a size-tiered byte compare; the stdlib's `indexOf` instead calls `compareImpl` at every candidate position. Case conversion checks the range is ASCII with one vector scan and folds a-z/A-Z in a single allocate-and-fold pass, where the stdlib over-allocates 3x, walks the Unicode special-case tables per code unit and then reallocates. View-producing ops (slice, trim, split) move two pointers instead of copying characters, so they avoid copying characters but still allocate one view object.
when_to_use: Substring search (indexOf, includes, replace) on haystacks of hundreds to thousands of UTF-16 units in AssemblyScript: 8.1-8.2x for indexOf/includes and 11x for replace on a 1,024-unit ASCII string (author's v0.2.2 chart).
ASCII case folding (toUpperCase/toLowerCase) of mostly-ASCII text such as headers, identifiers or keys: about 3.8-3.9x over the stdlib's Unicode-aware loop.
Tokenizing and trimming input (log lines, request lines, CSV fields) where most substrings are inspected and discarded rather than kept, so materialization is rare.
Text that already lives as UTF-8 bytes (WASI, network, JSON payloads): `str8.fromBuffer` slices and searches it without transcoding to UTF-16.

An existing AssemblyScript codebase that can try the `as-str/auto` transform, which turns safe internal string locals into allocation-free packed spans without source edits (measure on your own workload, as the README advises).
when_not_to_use: Cheap per-call queries: length, charAt, at, codePointAt and substr measured 0.8-0.9x and startsWith/endsWith 0.7-0.8x of native on the author's chart; slice, substring, split, equals, repeat and concat are about 1.0x.
Non-ASCII text in toUpperCase/toLowerCase: the fast path bails out and the view is materialized and passed to the native method, which adds a copy over calling native directly.

Code that needs JavaScript String semantics or passes strings across many API boundaries: semantics mirror AssemblyScript's String, views are a distinct type, and every boundary crossing costs a `toString()` copy.
Long-lived small slices of large inputs: a view keeps its whole backing string reachable, so a retained 10-character view pins the full source buffer.
Projects that need a proven dependency: single author, 1 star, no issues filed, 11 npm releases between 24 June and 30 July 2026, and the published charts predate the v0.4-0.6 transform rewrite.

integration.form: module (npm package of AssemblyScript source, plus optional asc transforms as-str/global, as-str/auto, as-str/single)
integration.dependencies: utf-as ^0.3.1 (UTF-8/UTF-16 encode and decode); peer dependency assemblyscript >=0.28.10
integration.min_toolchain: AssemblyScript asc 0.28.10+ (benchmarked with ^0.28.18); SIMD tier needs --enable simd, otherwise the SWAR tier is compiled
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly host that runs asc output; SIMD path needs Wasm SIMD128 support (chosen at compile time via ASC_FEATURE_SIMD); views rely on AssemblyScript's non-moving GC
integration.thread_safety: not documented (views are plain GC objects; AssemblyScript modules are single-threaded per instance)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the free functions take a native string and return the same results as String methods (differential-fuzzed per the README), and as-str/auto rewrites native string code automatically, but `str` is a separate type and view results must be materialized with toString() wherever a native string is required

gotchas: lastIndexOf is not SIMD/SWAR accelerated at HEAD: util.ts `lastIndexOf` is a scalar backward loop that only checks the first code unit before the tail compare, although the README's Architecture section says `findUnit` powers it; the throughput chart accordingly shows identical SWAR and SIMD bars (28 Mops/s), and its 2.5x comes from skipping the stdlib's per-position compareImpl call.

'Without allocating' applies only to the transforms' packed spans: every `str.slice`, `trim`, `split` piece is a heap-allocated 3-field Str object (the Architecture section says a view op is exactly one allocation), which is why view ops chart at 1.0-1.5x rather than large gains.

replaceAll scans the haystack twice (a counting pass, then a copy pass, each calling indexOf until no match), so it gains 3.5x versus replace's 11x; str.replace and replaceAll also return a fresh copy when nothing matches, whereas the stdlib returns the original string.

Benchmark scope: one 1,024-unit ASCII string with the needle at code unit 953 (8 pad + 21 x 45-unit phrase, derived from str.bench.ts) and one 'n' false candidate per phrase; no non-ASCII input, short haystack or needle-dense case is measured, and the charts carry no CPU or OS.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the catalogued AssemblyScript entries, as-string-sink (MaxGraey) speeds up building strings by concatenation, and json-as (same author) parses JSON; pick as-str when the hot path reads existing text (search, trim, slice, case-fold), and combine it with as-string-sink when you also build output.
verified_claims_summary: First-party as-bench microbenchmarks (assembly/__benches__/str.bench.ts) at v0.2.2, commit a1025c0, 24 June 2026, V8 15.1.42, CPU not stated: on one 1,024-unit ASCII string the str SIMD build ran indexOf/includes about 0.75 vs 6.3 Mops/s (8.1-8.2x), lastIndexOf 11 vs 28 Mops/s (2.5x), toUpperCase/toLowerCase 3.8-3.9x and replace 11x faster than the AssemblyScript 0.28 stdlib String compiled with the same flags, while equals, compare, slice and most single-character queries were 0.7-1.1x. Both arms are in the same module, and the equality test uses a distinct copy so the stdlib's pointer-equality shortcut does not fire, so the comparison is fair, but it covers only that one input.
status_note: Active single-author project (npm 0.1.0 to 0.6.0 between 24 June and 30 July 2026, last commit 2026-07-30), MIT and small enough to vendor, but the only published charts are for v0.2.2, so re-measure on current code; the README's Flavors link (github.com/AssemblyScript/as-str) is a 404.
